title: scale-trigger-sensitivity-matrix-feb-2026
body:
Purpose and scope:
This working doc summarizes a focused set of autoscaling experiments run in Jan–Feb 2026 to quantify sensitivity of production SLOs and unit cost to common scale-trigger parameters. Goal: pick conservative, predictable defaults for Hosted API that minimize P99 latency regressions while keeping GPU headroom and cost acceptable across three primary regions (us-west1, eu-west1, ap-southeast1).

Background and motivation:
We saw two incidents in Q4 2025 where rapid bursty traffic caused canary models to queue requests for >2s P99 despite autoscaler adding nodes. Root cause analysis pointed at: aggressive min nodes=0 policies, conservative scale-up cooldowns, and triggers relying on single-metric thresholds (GPU utilization) which lag when queue builds. This experiment suite tests alternate triggers and cooldowns with synthetic burst patterns and real-week trace replay.

Methodology:
- Workloads: three templates: steady-sq (95% small requests, steady QPS), bursty-b2 (sudden 10x for 30–90s), and long-chat (longer context >2048 tokens causing higher per-request GPU usage).
- Source data: production traces from 2026-01 (sanitized), and synthetic Poisson bursts to stress scale-up.
- Simulator: redwood/infra/simulations branch; deterministic actor-based sim used to avoid cloud charges. Calibration done against real autoscaler behavior from Apr 2026 smoke tests.
- Metrics collected: P50/P95/P99 latency, request queue length, tail GPU utilization, nodes provisioned over time, cost delta (relative to baseline policy).
- Baseline policy: min_nodes=1, max_nodes=50, scale_up_trigger: 70% avg GPU util over 30s, scale_up_cooldown=60s, scale_down_trigger: 25% util for 120s, scale_down_cooldown=300s.

Experiment matrix (summary):
We explored three axis: min_nodes (0/1/2), trigger metric (GPU_util_avg / request_queue / hybrid), and cooldowns (short/medium/long). Each run labeled STxx. Key runs below: 
- ST01 (baseline)
- ST02: min_nodes=0, scale_up_trigger=70% util, cooldown_up=30s
- ST03: min_nodes=1, trigger=request_queue>40, cooldown_up=15s
- ST04: min_nodes=2, trigger=hybrid (queue>30 OR util>65%), cooldown_up=20s
- ST05: min_nodes=1, trigger=hybrid, cooldown_up=10s, cooldown_down=180s
- ST06: min_nodes=1, trigger=queue>20 with smoothing window=60s (aggressive smoothing)

Representative sensitivity matrix (excerpt):
Columns: Region | Workload | Policy | Peak P99 (ms) | Avg nodes during burst | Max queued requests | Cost delta vs baseline (%)
- us-west1 | bursty-b2 | ST01 (baseline) | 2100 | 18 | 460 | +0%
- us-west1 | bursty-b2 | ST02 (min0, short cooldown) | 3700 | 12 | 1200 | -11% (fewer nodes but queueing)
- us-west1 | bursty-b2 | ST03 (queue trigger) | 900 | 22 | 80 | +8%
- us-west1 | bursty-b2 | ST04 (min2, hybrid) | 700 | 25 | 30 | +14%
- eu-west1 | steady-sq | ST01 | 150 | 6 | 2 | 0%
- eu-west1 | long-chat | ST04 | 1100 | 14 | 5 | +12%
- ap-southeast1 | bursty-b2 | ST05 | 820 | 21 | 42 | +10%

Key observations (unique/important findings):
1) min_nodes=0 reduces cost but dramatically increases tail latency under short, high-concurrency bursts because cold-start capacity provisioning time (image pull + driver init) is non-negligible for GPUs. In sim we modeled cooled images at 30–45s; observed P99 increase up to 2x in bursty traffic (ST02).
2) Queue-based triggers (request_queue threshold) detect demand earlier than average GPU utilization and consistently reduced P99 by ~40–65% in burst scenarios (ST03 vs ST01). However, they slightly increase steady-state cost due to earlier/richer node retention.
3) Hybrid triggers (queue OR util) with modest min_nodes (>=1) provided the best tradeoff: stable tail latency with bounded cost increase (~8–15% depending on region).
4) Very short scale_up cooldowns (<15s) cause oscillation on mixed workloads: scaler spins nodes up and then immediately down in alternating patterns when request patterns have micro-bursts, increasing both cost and chance of contention. A cooldown of 15–30s is a reasonable middle ground in our tests.
5) Scale-down cooldowns are critical to avoid thrashing; aggressive downscales (<=60s) harmed tail latency on follow-up bursts. 180–300s down cooldowns reduced recoveries and overall cost inefficiencies.
6) Regional differences: ap-southeast1 has longer cold-start times in our environment (image registry replication lag + smaller warm pool) — recommend slightly larger min_nodes there. eu-west1 had more predictable CPU warmup, so it tolerated lower min nodes for steady workloads.

Detailed recommendations (per region):
- us-west1 (primary): recommended default: min_nodes=1, max_nodes=60, trigger=hybrid(queue>30 OR util_avg>65% over 20s), scale_up_cooldown=20s, scale_down_trigger=util_avg<30% for 180s, scale_down_cooldown=180s. Rationale: best P99 reduction with moderate cost increase; region has fast image pulls.
- eu-west1: recommended default: min_nodes=0 for strictly steady low-QPS customers; for shared hosted capacity use min_nodes=1, trigger=hybrid(queue>25 OR util>70%) with longer scale_down=240s. Rationale: lower baseline demand and reliable registry replication.
- ap-southeast1: recommended default: min_nodes=2, trigger=hybrid(queue>25 OR util>60%), scale_up_cooldown=30s, scale_down=300s. Rationale: higher cold start penalty, prefer more headroom.

Tradeoffs and expected impact:
- Cost: adopting hybrid triggers with min_nodes>=1 across regions increases baseline cost ~8–12% but reduces P99 by ~50–70% for bursty patterns. For customers on Dedicated/Private, these defaults are still conservative and can be tuned per-tenant.
- Reliability: reduced incident risk from queue buildup; fewer degraded customer requests and retries.
- Ops complexity: hybrid triggers add one more metric to monitor (request_queue). We'll need dashboarding and synthetic alert rules.

Monitoring and dashboards to add (actionable):
- New dashboard: autoscale-sensitivity: P99 vs queued requests vs nodes over last 24h (per-region).
- Alert: queued_requests>200 sustained 30s AND P99>1.5s -> paging.
- Synthetic test: every 4h run 60s 5x burst to check recovery and observe autoscaler behavior (fail if P99>1.2s or nodes_added<3).

Action items and owners:
- Implement hybrid trigger prototype in staging autoscaler (PR: GH: redwood/infra#4532) — owner: Diego Martinez — due 2026-03-02.
- Create new dashboards and alerts — owner: Lina Zhou — due 2026-02-26.
- Run limited rollout to 10% of Hosted API traffic in us-west1 using ST04 defaults — owner: Omar Haddad — due 2026-03-09.
- Post-rollout measurement and rollback plan (if P99 > +200ms or cost delta > +20% w/o user-visible improvement) — owner: Maya Patel — due 2026-03-16.

Risks and open questions:
- Our simulator assumes image pull times consistent with current snapshots; upstream registry changes could alter cold start. Need to validate in-cloud pre-rollout.
- Queue metric instrumentation granularity: current collection at 5s; smoothing/window size may change trigger sensitivity.
- Some enterprise customers require predictable billing — we should provide per-tenant autoscale profiles (conservative vs cost-optimized).

Appendix: notable raw numbers (selected runs) — for full CSV see GH linked artifact:
- ST02 (us-west1, bursty-b2): avg nodes 12 vs baseline 18, peak queued 1200, P99 3700ms, cost -11%
- ST03 (us-west1, bursty-b2): avg nodes 22, peak queued 80, P99 900ms, cost +8%
- ST04 (us-west1, bursty-b2): avg nodes 25, peak queued 30, P99 700ms, cost +14%

Conclusion:
Switching from pure-utilization triggers with min_nodes=0 to hybrid queue+util triggers and modest min_nodes materially improves tail latency for bursty workloads at a manageable cost increase. Recommended next step: land staging prototype (GH PR above), deploy synthetic canary and run 2-week limited rollout in us-west1 before company-wide default change.

Notes (for reviewers):
- This doc is an experimental working draft. If you copy results into a public doc, please cite GH simulation id and attach the CSV.
- Feedback requested on suggested thresholds and cooldown values; especially interested in alternative queue thresholds and smoothing options.
